name: Quiché
confidence_why: 3 independent first-hand descriptions agree (2 state the same rule, 0 refine it); none contradicts. Chichicastenango K'iche' is described separately below, with a different pattern.
catalog_citation: Henderson, Robert. 2012. Morphological alternations at the intonational phrase edge: The case of K'ichee'. Natural Language & Linguistic Theory 30(3): 741-787. Dordrecht: Springer. (Read from the author's preprint, 44 pp., downloaded from rhenderson.net via the Internet Archive the Internet Archive.)
catalog_quote: Stress falls on the final syllable of a prosodic word, unless that syllable is light non-root material, in which case it falls on the final root syllable. The first part of the generalization is that stress is attracted to the right edge of the prosodic word. Examples (83)–(84) show that stress falls on the rightmost syllable if it is a root syllable or a heavy affix.

new_statements.quote: In den heutigen Dialekten des Quiché hat die Betonung keinen Phonemstatus; sie fällt regelmäßig auf die letzte Silbe eines Wortes, nur einsilbige Partikeln sind teilweise unbetont (Nahualá: Mondloch 1978a: 9–10; Cantel: Fox 1965: 20).[Fn. 3:] Norman (1976: 56) gibt für Santa Catarina Ixtahuacán jedoch abweichend von Mondloch an, daß bei Worten mit auslautendem Kurzvokal die vorletzte Silbe betont sei. [p. 41 Fn. 1:] Langvokale kommen als erster Vokal nur dann vor, wenn sie auf die Folge /Vh/ zurückgehen, ansonsten ist in der unbetonten Silbe der Kontrast kurz vs. lang aufgehoben.
new_statements.translation: In the present-day dialects of Quiché, stress has no phonemic status; it falls regularly on the last syllable of a word, only monosyllabic particles are partly unstressed (Nahualá: Mondloch 1978a: 9-10; Cantel: Fox 1965: 20). [Fn. 3:] Norman (1976: 56), however, states for Santa Catarina Ixtahuacán, differing from Mondloch, that in words ending in a short vowel the penultimate syllable is stressed. [p. 41 fn. 1:] Long vowels occur as the first vowel [of a root] only when they go back to the sequence /Vh/; otherwise the short vs. long contrast is neutralised in the unstressed syllable.
new_statements.citation: Dürr, Michael (1986). Morphologie, Syntax und Textstrukturen des (Maya-)Quiche des Popol Vuh: linguistische Beschreibung eines kolonialzeitlichen Dokuments aus dem Hochland von Guatemala. Berlin. University of Berlin. xii+380 pp.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement and type as the catalog record (fixed final; catalog quote from Henderson 2012: stress on the final syllable of the prosodic word unless that syllable is light non-root material). Dürr's 'monosyllabic particles partly unstressed' is compatible with Henderson's non-root-material clause. Adds: stress explicitly non-phonemic; length neutralisation in unstressed syllables. Reports second-hand one dialect-specific dissent (Norman 1976, Santa Catarina Ixtahuacán: penult stress in short-vowel-final words), which the catalog does not mention. The statement is sourced to modern dialects (Mondloch 1978a, Fox 1965), not observed in the colonial text itself.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress in (modern) Quiché is non-phonemic and falls regularly on the last syllable of the word; monosyllabic particles may be unstressed. Dürr takes this from the modern dialect descriptions (Nahualá: Mondloch 1978a; Cantel: Fox 1965) and assumes it for the colonial Quiché of the Popol Vuh, whose orthography does not mark stress; he uses it to explain that vowel syncope hits pretonic syllables (p. 37), that particles/function words lose their final consonant phrase-internally in unstressed position (p. 38), and that the vowel-length contrast is neutralised in the unstressed (non-final) root syllable (p. 41 fn. 1).
new_statements.secondary_stress: nothing said about secondary stress ('Hauptbetonung' on p. 37 implies only the main stress is discussed)
new_statements.exceptions: (i) monosyllabic particles are partly unstressed; (ii) footnote 3: Norman (1976: 56) reports for the Santa Catarina Ixtahuacán dialect, against Mondloch, that words ending in a short vowel stress the penultimate syllable; (iii) length contrast neutralised in unstressed syllables (p. 41 fn. 1)
new_statements.identity_note: The work describes the colonial (16th-18th c.) Quiché of the Popol Vuh manuscript (Classical K'iche'); since the colonial orthography marks neither length nor stress, its stress paragraph is explicitly about the present-day dialects (Nahualá per Mondloch 1978a; Cantel per Fox 1965; footnote on Santa Catarina Ixtahuacán per Norman 1976) and is assumed to hold for the Popol Vuh language.

new_statements.quote: Stress in most dialects of K’iche’ is fixed on the final syllable (López Ixcoy 1997; Baird 2014). In at least some dialects three affixes fall outside of the domain of stress, resulting in stress falling on the penultimate syllable of some adjectives and verbs. [p. 59] ... Based on the impressionistic marking of stress in the corpus, the following generalizations emerge: 1. In non-verbs (nouns, adjectives, adverbs), stress falls on the final syllable, irrespective of syllable weight 2. In verbs, stress is assigned according to a hierarchy of syllable weights [p. 61] ... stress appears to falls on the left-most of the heaviest syllable type available, or in the case of no heavy syllables default to the right-most (final) syllable. [p. 68]
new_statements.citation: Wood, Elizabeth Anne. 2020. Vowels and stress in Chichicastenango K'iche'. MA thesis, University of Texas at Austin.
new_statements.locator: ch. 3 'Stress Pattern and Acoustic Cues to Stress': §3.2.1 p. 59; §3.3.1 p. 61; §3.3.1.2 pp. 64-68; §3.4 pp. 70-71; secondary stress p. 88

Master of Arts, UT Austin, August 2020 (an MA report, not strictly a thesis). In at least some dialects three affixes fall outside of the domain of stress..' (sec. 3.2.1, p. 59, the text); the two numbered generalizations '1. In non-verbs.. stress falls on the final syllable, irrespective of syllable weight 2. In verbs, stress is assigned according to a hierarchy of syllable weights' (sec. 3.3.1, p. 61, lines 2088-2092);…
new_statements.relation_note: The language-general statement (final stress in most dialects) agrees with the catalog's final primary stress. The dialect-specific findings are about Chichicastenango (and Nahualá comparison data), not San Andrés: Chichicastenango verbs would contradict a fixed: final syllable rule, and the suffix-domain exceptions refine it. The work gives no secondary-stress pattern, so the catalog's alternating secondaries (0101, 10101) are neither confirmed nor denied.
new_statements.rule_in_words: For K'iche' generally (citing López Ixcoy 1997 and Baird 2014): primary stress is fixed on the final syllable; in some dialects the suffixes -a (attributive adjective), -alaj (superlative) and dependent-mood -a lie outside the stress domain, giving surface penultimate stress in those words (Nahualá examples Table 3.1, p. 59; final stress otherwise, Table 3.2, p. 60). For the Chichicastenango dialect specifically (preliminary, impressionistic, 8 speakers): non-verbs have fixed final stress; verbs stress the leftmost peripheral-vowel closed syllable, else leftmost peripheral-vowel open syllable, else leftmost centralized-vowel closed syllable, else the final syllable, with person/aspect prefixes and status suffixes (-ik, -o, -u, -oq) outside the stress domain (pp. 64-68).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described: 'Since there is no description of secondary stress in this dialect, and addressing this would require a specific study and larger database, this question is left to future research.' (p. 88)
new_statements.exceptions: Suffixes -a, -alaj/-läj and dependent -a outside the stress domain (penult surface stress); Chichicastenango status suffixes never stressed (unlike Nahualá, where 'stress is final, and status suffixes are always stressed', p. 64); Chichicastenango verbs weight/quality-sensitive; author calls the Chichicastenango analysis 'very preliminary' (p. 71).
new_statements.identity_note: kich1263 is the San Andrés (Sajcabajá) dialect of K'iche'. Neither opened work describes it: Barrett 2002 is explicitly the Nahualá dialect (fn. 1); Wood 2020 describes Chichicastenango K'iche' with Nahualá comparison data and a language-general statement ('most dialects of K'iche'') that covers San Andrés only by implication. Baird 2014 (not opened) covers Nahualá, Zunil and Cantel according to Wood 2020 p. 60.

new_statements.quote: In K’ichee’ roots and stems, word-final CVC and CVV syllables receive primary stress. Secondary stress occurs in words of three or more syllables and falls on the initial syllable and consecutive alternating syllables moving left to right. Secondary stress does not occur on the penultimate or antepenultimate syllable (i.e. stress clash between secondary and primary stress is not allowed). [p. 1] ... Other consonants end in a light syllable, with primary stress falling on the penultimate syllable as shown in 3) below ... The phrase-medial cliticized forms demonstrate that the primary stress is actually a moraic trochee aligned at rightmost edge. The feet for secondary stress are syllabic trochees moving left to right. Stress clash and degenerate feet are prohibited [p. 2]

new_statements.relation_note: Same primary placement (final) for uncliticized words, but two differences from the catalog alternating stress from the right: (a) at four syllables Barrett's examples give 1001 (ètamab'ál, tìkoonijél), not 0101, because secondary feet are built left-to-right from the initial syllable with clash avoidance, not right-to-left from the primary; (b) primary stress is weight-conditioned (final heavy; penult when a phrase-medial clitic leaves a light final syllable), not fixed: final syllable. 2, 3 and 5-syllable shapes (01, 101, 10101) agree. Describes the Nahualá dialect, not San Andrés.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Nahualá dialect (fn. 1, field notes, consultant Gregorio Tum). Primary stress on the word-final syllable when it is heavy (CVC or CVV), which is the case for all roots and stems; analysed as a moraic trochee at the right edge, so that when a phrase-medial clitic leaves a light final syllable (imb'éb'i, kimb'éti) primary stress falls on the penult. Heaviness counts only word-finally ('CVV and CVC syllables in K'ichee' only count as heavy when they are word final', p. 3). Examples: porór, kajíb', tìnamít, k'òlok'ík, ètamab'ál, tìkoonijél, kàwunùnwutík.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: in words of three or more syllables, on the initial syllable and alternating syllables left to right (syllabic trochees), quantity-insensitive, never on the penult or antepenult (no clash): tìnamít (101), ètamab'ál and tìkoonijél (1001), kàwunùnwutík and kàtoqtòqiník (10101).
new_statements.exceptions: Cliticized verb forms: phrase-final clitics keep final heavy syllable and final stress (ìmb'e=bík, kìmb'e=tík); phrase-medial forms lose the final consonant, and non-glottal ones end light and take penultimate stress (imb'éb'i, kimb'éti); glottal-final ones show compensatory lengthening and keep final stress (ìmb'ewíi).
new_statements.identity_note: kich1263 is the San Andrés (Sajcabajá) dialect of K'iche'. Neither opened work describes it: Barrett 2002 is explicitly the Nahualá dialect (fn. 1); Wood 2020 describes Chichicastenango K'iche' with Nahualá comparison data and a language-general statement ('most dialects of K'iche'') that covers San Andrés only by implication. Baird 2014 (not opened) covers Nahualá, Zunil and Cantel according to Wood 2020 p. 60.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-contrastive and falls regularly on the final syllable of the word in the modern K'iche' dialects (documented for Nahualá and Cantel, both West Central); monosyllabic particles may be unstressed. The author states this for the modern dialects and assumes it for the colonial Quiché of the Popol Vuh, whose orthography does not show stress; pretonic short vowels tend to be deleted.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing on secondary stress (the term 'Hauptbetonung' on p. 37 implies a main stress but no secondary-stress pattern is described).
new_statements.exceptions: Monosyllabic particles are partly unstressed; fn. 3: Norman (1976: 56) reports for Santa Catarina Ixtahuacán that words ending in a short vowel stress the penultimate syllable (a dialect-specific deviation from Mondloch's Nahualá description).
new_statements.identity_note: Dürr 2003 describes the colonial Quiché of the Popol Vuh (16th c., Santa Cruz del Quiché / highland Guatemala) but its stress statement is explicitly about the present-day dialects, sourced to Nahualá (Mondloch 1978a) and Cantel (Fox 1965), both within Glottolog's West Central K'iche' (kich1266), with a footnote on Santa Catarina Ixtahuacán (Norman 1976), also West Central. Baird 2014 (unread) reportedly uses Nahualá speakers.

readall_conflicts: Barrett 2002 (Nahualá) and the catalog agree on final primary stress and on the 2-, 3- and 5-syllable shapes, but disagree on secondary stress at four syllables: Barrett's initial-plus-alternating left-to-right pattern with clash avoidance yields 1001 (ètamab'ál, tìkoonijél) where the catalog gives 0101; Barrett also treats the primary as a right-edge moraic trochee requiring a heavy (CVC/CVV) final, so cliticized phrase-medial forms with a light final syllable take penultimate stress. Wood 2020 agrees with the catalog for the language in general (final stress in most dialects) but reports for Chichicastenango that only non-verbs have fixed final stress while verbs stress the leftmost heaviest syllable by a quality-and-closure hierarchy with final stress as the default; she also notes suffixes (-a, -alaj, dependent -a) outside the stress domain that produce surface penult stress in Nahualá, and no description of secondary stress. Wood's 'irrespective of syllable weight' (Chichicastenango non-verbs) versus Barrett's heavy-final requirement (Nahualá) is a difference of dialect and of analysis rather than a conflict on surface data, since uncliticized roots and stems end in heavy syllables in Barrett's data. Baird 2014 could not be opened. Only Barrett 2002 could be opened. Within it, primary stress is final for all roots and stems (every root/stem ends in a heavy CVC/CVV syllable), shifting to the penult only when a phrase-medial clitic leaves a light final syllable — i.e. fin…

sources.quote: In den heutigen Dialekten des Quiché hat die Betonung keinen Phonemstatus; sie fällt regelmäßig auf die letzte Silbe eines Wortes, nur einsilbige Partikeln sind teilweise unbetont (Nahualá: Mondloch 1978a: 9–10; Cantel: Fox 1965: 20).[Fn. 3:] Norman (1976: 56) gibt für Santa Catarina Ixtahuacán jedoch abweichend von Mondloch an, daß bei Worten mit auslautendem Kurzvokal die vorletzte Silbe betont sei. [p. 41 Fn. 1:] Langvokale kommen als erster Vokal nur dann vor, wenn sie auf die Folge /Vh/ zurückgehen, ansonsten ist in der unbetonten Silbe der Kontrast kurz vs. lang aufgehoben.
sources.locator: p. 28 (ch. 3.1 'Phoneminventar', PDF page 40) with footnote 3; supporting remarks p. 37 (3.3.2, rule 3 'Vokalausfall'), p. 38 (rule 6) and p. 41 fn. 1 (3.5 'Morphemstruktur')
sources.note: Same placement and type as the catalog record (fixed final; catalog quote from Henderson 2012: stress on the final syllable of the prosodic word unless that syllable is light non-root material). Dürr's 'monosyllabic particles partly unstressed' is compatible with Henderson's non-root-material clause. Adds: stress explicitly non-phonemic; length neutralisation in unstressed syllables. Reports second-hand one dialect-specific dissent (Norman 1976, Santa Catarina Ixtahuacán: penult stress in short-vowel-final words), which the catalog does not mention. The statement is sourced to modern dialects…

sources.citation: Wood, Elizabeth Anne. 2025. Predictable vowel deletion in content words and variable vowel deletion in function words in Chichicastenango K'iche'. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 55(3): 465-502. doi:10.1017/S0025100325100765 (open access)
sources.quote: 'Primary stress is word-final in non-verbs in Chichicastenango K'iche', with the exclusion of two extrametrical suffixes: the superlative /-@l@X/ and the suffix /-Ik/ ... Stress is non-final in some unadapted Spanish loanwords' (p. 467). 'In verbs, stress is sensitive to vowel quality and syllable shape. Stress falls on the left-most syllable containing either a tense vowel or a coda, or if there are none, on the final syllable. The stress domain excludes most inflectional morphemes' (p. 468). No secondary stress. Refines the plain-final picture for one (innovative) dialect; says nothing about

sources.quote: Stress in most dialects of K’iche’ is fixed on the final syllable (López Ixcoy 1997; Baird 2014). In at least some dialects three affixes fall outside of the domain of stress, resulting in stress falling on the penultimate syllable of some adjectives and verbs. [p. 59] ... Based on the impressionistic marking of stress in the corpus, the following generalizations emerge: 1. In non-verbs (nouns, adjectives, adverbs), stress falls on the final syllable, irrespective of syllable weight 2. In verbs, stress is assigned according to a hierarchy of syllable weights [p. 61] ... stress appears to falls on the left-most of the heaviest syllable type available, or in the case of no heavy syllables default to the right-most (final) syllable. [p. 68]

sources.citation: Nielsen, Kuniko. 2005. Kiche intonation. UCLA Working Papers in Phonetics 104: 45-60 (eScholarship 52n7344j).
sources.quote: 'Stress in Kiche is always word-final (Larsen, 1988). Stressed syllables are marked by pitch, duration, intensity, and loudness. Most importantly, Kiche stress is marked by a rise of the fundamental frequency (F0) on the stressed syllable.' Enclitics do not shift stress (k-u-pús=wi); some recent loans have non-final stress (mángo, pláto); K'iche' analysed as an edge language with lexical stress-driven pitch accent (LH*).
sources.locator: p. 46 (p. 2-3), section 1-2; Cantel (West Central) dialect, one speaker, instrumental
sources.note: Instrumental (one Cantel speaker): confirms word-final primary stress cued by F0 rise; reports only an AP-initial 'rhythmic high', no iambic alternation.

sources.quote: 'In K'ichee' roots and stems, word-final CVC and CVV syllables receive primary stress. Secondary stress occurs in words of three or more syllables and falls on the initial syllable and consecutive alternating syllables moving left to right. Secondary stress does not occur on the penultimate or antepenultimate syllable' (e.g. tìkoonijél, kàtikrìkiník). When a phrase-medial clitic loses its final consonant and ends light, primary stress is penultimate (imb'éb'i, kimb'éti): 'the primary stress is actually a moraic trochee aligned at rightmost edge'.
sources.locator: pp. 1-2, section 1 'Stress patterns in K'ichee'' (Nahualá dialect)
sources.note: The one primary description of K'iche' secondary stress (Nahualá): initial + alternating L-to-R, no clash (tìnamít, ètamab'ál, kàwunùnwutík) => stress placement coded per word length as 01 101 1001 10101 (1 = a stressed syllable), contradicting the record's 0101 for 4-syllable words.

sources.quote: In most Quiche verbs, the final vowel is the one that receives primary stress (Norman 1976:56). In utterances where the verb is final, the verb's stressed syllable is also utterance-final. [...] This behavior can be tied to the way that stress shifts in the two environments; in clause-medial positions, the word stems are stressed, whereas in clause-final positions the terminations receive primary stress.
sources.locator: pp. 591, 597; also p. 586 ('Each termination receives primary stress, except dependent intransitive /-a/') and p. 594
sources.note: marginal: Child-acquisition study arguing that Quiché syllable structure and stress rules (final stress) promote early acquisition of verb terminations; stress is invoked as an explanatory factor rather than described as the object.
